job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I cycle to the plant in Stockport, about twenty-five minutes. I'm a junior test engineer at a company that makes hearing aids. I run batches of new circuit boards through a rig, read the numbers, and write up which ones pass. By lunch I'm usually eating a cheese sandwich with Priya, who sits at the next bench. Evenings I'm home in Salford with two flatmates, cooking big pots of dal and watching badly dubbed football.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there, and what did you study?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering at Manchester, graduated with a 2:1. My final project was a small battery monitor for e-bikes, and I did a ten-week summer placement at a power supply firm. The hearing aid job came from a careers fair stall. My mum is a nurse and has always said get a trade that people need, and she lent me a deposit for the room. I owe about thirteen thousand in loan and have around six weeks of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what engineers have been saying for years. Tools get better, and the hard bits still need a person who understands the circuit. At work I'd nod and keep using the AI assistant for tidying test reports, which I do every now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fairly safe. Hearing aids are regulated, and every test result has to be signed off by a named person, so there's a human in the chain. My worry is more about money, because I'm still paying back the loan and the room costs a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd ask to take the next evening course our company pays for, on medical device standards, since it makes me harder to replace. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month, and I'd try to get on a rota so I'd learn the other test rigs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay. I'd still be a bit tight on money but not frightened about work. I'd go to bed feeling normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your day AI would touch in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The write-up, mostly. I spend maybe a quarter of my time turning numbers into a report, and a tool already does a decent first draft. I'd be glad of that. The rig and the sign-off stay with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job feels safe. What would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm lost its main contract with the health service. A small company like ours lives on two or three big customers, and I'd be one of the youngest. That has nothing to do with AI, and it's the thing I think about on a bad day.

say: Tools get better, but hard bits still need someone who **understands the circuit**.
I'd keep using the AI assistant for **report tidying**.
think: Hearing aid testing is **regulated**, and a named person must sign off every result.
My real pressure is the **loan** and the cost of my room.
do: Take the company-paid evening course on **medical device standards**.
Keep **saving** about two hundred pounds a month.
Learn the other test rigs on a **rota**.
feel: **Fairly okay**, tight on money but not frightened about work.
S0.quote: I'd still be a bit tight on money but not frightened about work. I'd go to bed feeling normal.
fieldNote: Her **regulated** sector gives real protection and she says exactly why.
The one thing she fears is a lost contract, which is a **small-firm** risk, not an AI one.
Already uses AI for report drafts, a steady and practical approach.

steps.text: Sign up for the medical device standards evening course
Put 200 pounds a month into savings
Keep running board tests and writing reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, but put the human checks in writing. If a tool writes the test plan, somebody still needs to understand it, and I'd like that somebody to be me. Online I'd back stronger rules on what AI can sign off, and I'd say the workers affected should be in the room when firms decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy, because writing test plans and reading results is exactly the work they say AI does well. Our team has four juniors and one senior, and I could see the firm hiring one fewer next year. I think I'd survive, but I might not get the rig time I need to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools properly rather than now and then, and learn what they get wrong, so I'm the one who checks them. I'd ask my manager for a place on the new product line where boards are built by hand, because hands-on testing is slower to automate. I'd also join the union branch our site has, which I've ignored so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I'd feel like I was running a race where the track moves. But I'd also feel I had a fair chance because I'm adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, honestly. She's got a mortgage and her whole job is writing test reports for a manager who loves software. If they cut one, I think it's her desk, and I'd feel awful because I'd be less likely to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does using AI properly look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let it draft the test plan, then I'd run the first ten boards by hand to see if it's right. Every time it's wrong, I'd write down how. By next summer I'd have a notebook of its mistakes, and that's the sort of thing that makes me useful.

say: Put the **human checks** in writing, and let workers in the room.
I'd back stronger rules on what AI can **sign off**.
think: Writing test plans is the work AI does well, so the firm may hire **one fewer** junior.
I'd probably survive but may lose **rig time** to grow.
do: Use AI tools **properly** and keep a log of what they get wrong.
Ask for a place on the **hand-built** product line.
feel: **Unsettled**, like a race on a moving track, but with a fair chance.
S1.quote: If a tool writes the test plan, somebody still needs to understand it, and I'd like that somebody to be me.
fieldNote: Her plan is to be the person who **checks** the AI, a smart use of adaptability.
Worry is for a colleague first: Priya, who has a mortgage.
Steady rather than eager: she wants proof from her own notebook.

steps.text: Draft test plans with AI and test the first ten boards by hand
Ask to move to the hand-built product line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone, and the first people hurt will be people like me who've just started. At work I'd ask what the firm plans and whether it would promise anything in writing. Online I'd push for income support and for public money to retrain people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my chance of a long career here drops a lot. Writing test code and reading results, which is half my job, goes to AI in 2028. The hands-on rig work lasts maybe until 2031, but a company that can run on AI for thinking work will hire fewer juniors in the meantime. I'd say I'm at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra and move my savings target up to three months of costs. I'd ask my mum if I could move home for a few months if it came to it, and she'd say yes before I finished asking. I'd also learn the hardware side as hard as I can, soldering, repairs, the rig, because that part holds out for a bit longer. And I'd write to my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit angry. But I'm not frozen, because I'd have a list. I think the list is what keeps me going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call her after her night shift and say, Mum, I think they'll cut juniors within the year. She'd say, you can always come home, and then she'd say, have you eaten. And I'd cry a little, because I'm twenty-two and still need that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms that race ahead, and governments who've watched without a plan. I don't think anyone is being evil. I just think nobody's in charge, and the people at the bottom of the ladder pay.

say: Two years is too fast, and **new starters** will be hurt first.
I'd ask for **promises in writing** and push for retraining money.
think: The test code and results half of my job goes to AI in **2028**.
The firm may hire **fewer juniors** well before robots reach hands-on rig work.
do: Raise my savings target to **three months** of costs.
Learn **soldering, repairs** and the rig properly.
Write to my **MP** about income support.
feel: **Worried and angry**, but a list keeps me going.
S2.quote: I just think nobody's in charge, and the people at the bottom of the ladder pay.
fieldNote: Mood is **anxious**, not alarmed: she has a list, family support and some hands-on work left.
Emotional centre is her mother, a night-shift nurse.
Does not blame villains, only a lack of anyone steering.

steps.text: Raise my savings target to three months of costs
Practise soldering and board repairs at the bench every week
Write to my MP about retraining and income support
Agree with my mum that I can move home if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say, is long enough to do something sensible, so let's actually do it. At work I'd ask for training paths, and online I'd back a public fund and rules on what AI can run alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be more hopeful than with two years. I'd be 27 in 2031 and might have paid off a lot of the loan, and I'd have six years of experience, which is worth something as a person who checks the AI. But I'd keep watching, because five years goes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job for two or three years and get chartered, which is a professional qualification that makes me harder to replace. I'd also save for a flat deposit, but slowly, and maybe change my plan if things look worse. I'd keep using AI at work and learn the safety side of it, because I think that's where the engineering work will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, though not scared. I'd feel like there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why chartered status and not something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a signature from a chartered engineer still carries legal weight. If AI does the thinking, someone still has to be the named human who answers when it goes wrong. I'd rather be that person than the one who gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm stopped hiring graduates and started shrinking. Then I'd look outside, probably at a regulator or a hospital engineering team, where the job is about safety, not output. I'd also take a break from the flat deposit and keep the cash.

say: Five years is long enough to do something sensible, so let's **actually do it**.
I'd ask for **training paths** and back a public fund.
think: With six years behind me I'd be useful as the person who **checks the AI**.
Five years goes **quickly**, so I'd keep watching.
do: Work towards **chartered engineer** status over two or three years.
Save slowly for a flat **deposit** and keep cash flexible.
Learn the **safety side** of AI at work.
feel: **Cautious**, but not scared, because there's a path.
S3.quote: Someone still has to be the named human who answers when it goes wrong. I'd rather be that person than the one who gets replaced.
fieldNote: Gives the first concrete **career strategy** of the interview.
Sees the engineer's legal liability as protection.
Keeps an **exit plan** in mind: a regulator or hospital engineering team, if the firm stops hiring graduates.

steps.text: Start the chartered engineer application with the institution
Save a flat deposit slowly, keeping cash flexible
Learn how to test and audit AI tools at work
Look at hospital engineering teams if hiring stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it gives us time to build proper training and rules, and I'd tell friends who are about to start degrees to pick what they enjoy. At work I'd talk about career paths, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably a senior engineer with a flat, and I'd have lived through lots of smaller changes. I'd still keep some money aside, though, because I know a long timeline can end in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my career and take on a team-leading role in about five years. I'd also keep learning how the tools work, and I might do a part-time master's in AI safety if the firm helped pay. I'd carry on saving for the deposit and buy a place by thirty if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit excited, even. I'd probably have the energy to enjoy my twenties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long runway change what you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My brother, Daniel, is in sixth form and wants to do engineering. With ten years, I'd tell him to go ahead, but to learn how to work with the tools and to get hands-on experience in the summers. In the two-year world I'd say something very different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in feeling calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I stop paying attention. Ten years can turn into eight, and the date can move. I'd put a reminder in my diary every January to ask myself if I'm still on track.

say: Ten years gives us time to build **proper training** and rules.
I'd tell friends starting degrees to pick what they **enjoy**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and probably a **senior engineer** with a flat.
A long timeline can end in a **rush**, so I'd keep some money aside.
do: Aim for a **team-leading role** in about five years.
Do a part-time master's in **AI safety** if the firm helps pay.
Save for a **deposit** and buy by thirty if I can.
feel: **Calm**, a bit excited, with energy to enjoy my twenties.
S4.quote: Ten years can turn into eight, and the date can move. I'd put a reminder in my diary every January to ask myself if I'm still on track.
fieldNote: **Calm** is earned here: a secure plan, steady money and time.
Her brother Daniel appears as the person she would advise differently across scenarios.

steps.text: Aim for a team-leading role at the plant in five years
Apply for a part-time AI safety master's with company funding
Save for a flat deposit and buy by thirty
Tell my brother Daniel to get summer hands-on experience

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one scares me most, because nothing could be in place by then. What would help is a promise from the firm in writing, public money for retraining, and some kind of income support. If I could keep the loan from growing, I'd feel much better.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people my age get told to adapt as if it's a personal skill. I'm happy to adapt, and I do, but I'd like the rules and the safety net to adapt too.

headlineQuote: I'm happy to adapt, and I do, but I'd like the rules and the safety net to adapt too.
portrait: Amira Garcia is **22**, a junior test engineer at a hearing aid maker, living in a shared flat in Salford.
She did electrical engineering at Manchester, owes about **thirteen thousand** and has six weeks of costs saved.
She's progressive and steady: she uses **AI now and then**, and wants proof before she changes habits.
Her mood runs from calm to **anxious** in the two-year world, where her mum's spare room is her fallback.
She plans to be the **named human** who checks AI, through chartered status and safety work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **nothing** would be in place for graduates.
whatWouldHelp: A written **promise** from the firm, public money for retraining and some income support.
